metadata.note: The Denver & Rio Grande's original 1881-83 narrow-gauge route from Salida over Marshall Pass to Gunnison, through the Black Canyon of the Gunnison to Montrose, and on to Grand Junction -- the D&RG's first line to reach Utah, opened in stages: Salida-Gunnison June 21 1881, Gunnison-Montrose September 8 1882, Montrose-Grand Junction March 1883. This through route to Salt Lake City lasted only until the D&RG completed its new standard-gauge line over Tennessee Pass in November 1890, after which Marshall Pass/Black Canyon became a secondary narrow-gauge branch. The three legs then diverged in how long they lasted: the Gunnison-Montrose (Black Canyon) passenger service ended first, in August 1936, when trains 315/316 were cut back to Salida-Gunnison only; Salida-Gunnison itself (renamed the Shavano in 1937) lasted until November 24, 1940. The Montrose-Grand Junction leg had a separate history: it was standard-gauged in 1906 (severing its narrow-gauge connection to the Marshall Pass system except via a Montrose interchange) and continued to carry a named passenger train (the Mountaineer, from 1936) until that train was cut back to terminate at Grand Junction on February 1, 1951. Freight continued on all three legs well beyond their passenger end dates -- Marshall Pass was formally abandoned in 1953 and scrapped in 1955, the Black Canyon line was abandoned in stages 1949-1955 and its route substantially flooded by Blue Mesa Dam (1966) and Morrow Point Dam (1968), and Montrose-Grand Junction remains an active Union Pacific freight line today -- none of that freight-only or post-flooding history is drawn on the map, per CLAUDE.md Rule 1. Each corridor is split into two features at August 1, 1921, the date the bankrupt Denver & Rio Grande Railway was reorganized as the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad (old stockholders received nothing, so this is treated as a genuine ownership change per CLAUDE.md Rule 4), giving six features total. The Gunnison-Crested Butte branch is out of scope for this file (handled separately).

geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API, overpass-api.de): railway=rail/abandoned/disused/razed/construction ways queried across three bounding boxes covering Salida-Gunnison, Gunnison-Montrose, and Montrose-Grand Junction. Ways were filtered to those tagged old_railway_operator=D&RGW (or operator containing 'D&RGW'/'Rio Grande') and by name, excluding unrelated lines captured in the same bboxes: the Denver, South Park & Pacific/CB&Q 'South Park Line' and Alpine Tunnel Road (a competing, geographically overlapping route to Gunnison via a different pass, never D&RG), the D&RGW's Tennessee Pass Subdivision (a different, still-standard-gauge pass, not part of Marshall Pass), the Monarch Branch/Monarch Spur Trail (a limestone-quarry spur near Salida, not part of the through route), the Lake City Branch (a spur off this line at Sapinero, not part of the Montrose-bound route), and the Ouray Branch/Uncompahgre River Walk (a spur south from Montrose to Ouray, not part of the Grand Junction-bound route). Remaining ways were assembled into a routing graph (endpoints/vertices snapped to 5 decimal places, edges weighted by haversine distance) and connected with Dijkstra shortest-path between Salida, Gunnison, Montrose and Grand Junction. The resulting traced lengths matched the documented mileages closely on all three legs (see the per-leg entries below).

Salida-Gunnison (Marshall Pass): traced length ~72.5 route-miles against a documented 73.8 miles (98% match). Two short gaps in OSM's abandoned-railway tagging near Poncha Junction/Poncha Springs -- about 4.7 miles (7.5 km) between Salida and a fragment near the old Poncha Junction substation, and about 1.5 miles (2.5 km) between that fragment and the continuous 'Marshall Pass Road' abandoned-railway tagging further southwest -- are bridged as straight-line approximations (~8% of this feature's length). Everything else on this leg is real-traced from OSM's 'Marshall Pass Road' abandoned-railway tagging (old_railway_operator=D&RGW) and connecting 'Salida to Alamosa'/'Rainbow (Crest Section)' tagged trackage shared with the separate Poncha Pass line near Salida.

Gunnison-Montrose (Black Canyon): traced length 62.9 route-miles against a documented 62.9 miles (exact match). Fully real-traced from OSM's 'Denver & Rio Grande Western Abandoned Railroad' tagging, with no bridging needed -- this includes the section through and now substantially under the Blue Mesa/Morrow Point reservoirs, where OSM still carries the abandoned-railway alignment (surveyed/historically documented former grade) even though the physical track and much of the roadbed no longer exists there.

Montrose-Grand Junction: traced length 72.7 route-miles against a documented ~73-74 miles (near-exact match). Fully real-traced with no bridging needed, using OSM's active-rail tagging for this still-operating freight line: 'Montrose Industrial Lead' near Montrose and 'UP North Fork Subdivision' (old_railway_operator=D&RGW) on to Grand Junction.

Backtrack/self-intersection check: performed on all three Dijkstra-routed paths before simplification, using cumulative along-path distance (not point index) to separate genuine nearby-but-distant points from routing artifacts -- flagged any pair of points at least 15 path-indices and at least ~800m-2km apart along the path whose direct straight-line distance was under ~250m. No node was revisited in any of the three shortest paths (a structural guarantee of Dijkstra on a simple positive-weight graph), and the traced lengths came in at or slightly under the documented mileages rather than over them, which is inconsistent with an out-and-back doubling-back bug. The handful of flagged close-point pairs (concentrated near mile markers matching Marshall Pass's and Cerro Summit's well-documented horseshoe/switchback curves) are real mountain-railroad grade geometry, not a tracing artifact.

Geometry was simplified with Ramer-Douglas-Peucker (15m tolerance) after routing, to reduce point count while preserving switchback/loop shape; simplified lengths differ from the pre-simplification routed lengths by well under 1%.
not_yet_sourced: Exact frequency/timetable for any era beyond the single 1934 timetable snippet found (train 315/316 Salida-Montrose, with a same-day standard-gauge connection Montrose-Grand Junction); headway_min values throughout this file are a rough once-daily-round-trip estimate, not a sourced frequency.

The identity, name, and frequency of the standard-gauge Montrose-Grand Junction connecting train between 1906 (when that segment was standard-gauged) and 1936 (when the named Mountaineer began) -- only its existence in 1934 is confirmed.
Whether the Salida-Gunnison-Montrose narrow-gauge trains carried a name before 'Shavano' (1937); train numbers 315/316 are documented but an earlier name, if any, was not found.

The exact date the Gunnison-Cimarron-Montrose segment's freight-only remnant was fully scrapped (sources give 1953 approval and 'roughly two years later', i.e. ~1955, for the pull-up, without a precise date).

Whether any of the three legs saw named excursion, work, or railfan specials after their regular passenger end dates and before the flooding/freight-abandonment dates noted above; none were found, so none are drawn, but the absence of a source is not the same as confirmation none ran.
The Gunnison-Crested Butte branch, which shares this company/color but is out of scope for this file (a separate agent/file is understood to cover it).

segments.note: D&RGW era (reorganized from the D&RG August 1, 1921). Trains 315/316 continued to run Salida–Montrose daily through the Black Canyon and over Cerro Summit until August 1936, when the Gunnison–Montrose portion was discontinued -- ending passenger service on this segment. Freight over Cerro Summit east to Sapinero continued until 1949; the remaining Cedar Creek Branch stub was last used November 1952 and abandoned 1953; the rest of the former narrow-gauge main east of Sapinero was approved for abandonment in 1953 and pulled roughly two years later (not drawn -- freight only, see CLAUDE.md Rule 1). Much of this segment (Sapinero eastward toward Gunnison, and the most scenic canyon section) was later flooded by Blue Mesa Dam (completed 1966) and Morrow Point Dam (completed 1968).

segments.note: Line laid north from Montrose through Delta, reaching Grand Junction in March 1883 and completing the D&RG's narrow-gauge transcontinental connection (with the Rio Grande Western Railway) to Salt Lake City, Utah. Part of the original through route until the standard-gauge Tennessee Pass line opened in November 1890. Frequency assumed roughly one daily round trip; unsourced.

segments.note: Named the Mountaineer from 1936, running Denver–Montrose. Cut back to terminate at Grand Junction on February 1, 1951, ending passenger service on the Montrose–Grand Junction segment specifically (the Mountaineer itself continued Denver–Grand Junction to 1959). The line remains active for freight today as Union Pacific's North Fork Subdivision (Grand Junction–Delta) and the Montrose Industrial Lead (Delta–Montrose) -- not drawn past 1951, freight only, see CLAUDE.md Rule 1.
